title: Tyndale's plow
hookLine: Tyndale died so a ploughboy could read the Bible in English; many translations followed, KJV and Douay-Rheims among them

lines: A BOY WHO DRIVES THE PLOW.
cards: England, the 1520s. A young scholar named William Tyndale, who reads Greek and Hebrew, gets into an argument with a churchman.
The story goes that Tyndale told him, if God spared his life, he'd see to it that a boy who drives the plow would know more of the scriptures than he did.
Translating the Bible into English without church permission was forbidden, so Tyndale left England for good. In Germany, in 1526, he printed a New Testament in English, small enough to hide.

Copies were smuggled across the sea in bales of cloth, and many were burned. Nine years later, he was betrayed and arrested in Antwerp, and in 1536, near Brussels, he was strangled and his body burned.

teach.b: Every Bible in English is a carrying-across, from Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek. Before Tyndale, followers of John Wycliffe had copied English Bibles by hand, translated from Latin.
Tyndale went back to the original languages, and he had an ear. He gave English words and phrases it still uses: Passover. Scapegoat.

teach.h: PASSOVER, SCAPEGOAT, LET THERE BE LIGHT.
teach.b: Let there be light. The salt of the earth.
The King James Bible of 1611 leaned heavily on him; scholars estimate most of its New Testament is his. So when you've heard the King James quoted on this path, you've often been hearing Tyndale.
English Catholics made their own translation too, in exile in France, from the Latin: the Rheims New Testament in 1582 and the Douai Old Testament decades later.
That's the Douay-Rheims, the Catholic Bible in English for centuries.

teach.h: A VIOLENT AGE ON EVERY SIDE.
teach.b: It was a violent age on every side. Protestants and Catholics were both put to death for their faith. Thomas More, who wrote fiercely against Tyndale, was himself executed by Henry the Eighth a year before Tyndale died.
Christians of every church remember their own martyrs from that time. What nearly all Christians share now is the conviction that anyone should be able to read the Bible in their own language.
Today it has been translated in full into hundreds of languages, and in part into thousands more. Every one cost someone years; some cost a life.

how: Christians read the Bible in many translations; Protestants often use versions descended from Tyndale and the King James, Catholics use approved Catholic translations descended from the Douay-Rheims tradition, and Bible societies of many churches work to translate it into every language.

o: carrying words across into another language
copying a holy book out by hand, word by word
explaining what a hard passage really means

games.q: who carried what across — tap the pairs.

s: the King James Version was the first English Bible
Wycliffe's followers and Tyndale came first. the King James leaned heavily on Tyndale.
Tyndale translated from Greek and Hebrew, not Latin
he went back to the original languages.
only one side put people to death in those years
Protestants and Catholics were both executed. Thomas More died a year before Tyndale.

games.q: you're William Tyndale. the church authorities in England won't give you permission to translate the Bible into English. what do you do?
o: give up and teach Greek instead.
leave England and translate in secret abroad.
translate from Latin, as others did.
games.why: he left England and printed his New Testament in Germany in 1526. copies were smuggled home, and he was executed ten years later, in 1536.

practice: Remember who taught you to read: a parent with a picture book, a first-grade teacher, an older sibling, a librarian, someone who pointed at letters until they became words.
See their face if you can, and think what that one gift has opened for you since. If you pray, give thanks for them by name; if you don't, just feel grateful.

wordCard.voice: Translation. From the Latin for carried across. The work that brought the Bible from Hebrew and Greek into English, at great cost.

orig.note: Latin: a carrying across, from trans, across, and latus, carried.

carryVoice: Your line: words cost someone something. Tomorrow, a whole new stretch begins: giving and singing.

sources.ref: John Foxe, Acts and Monuments (the ploughboy saying and Tyndale's last words)
